rv.q: You emerge numb. Yet it grips completely – a must-see. … 28 years on, it is clearly grappling with hard, enduring truths about human nature. … general, she grasps that despite the required gory spectacle, less is more.
It's the theatrical equivalent of a poke in the eye with a sharp stick – and starts with just that: a syringe jabbed into the eyeball of an apparent junkie, by a sadistic physician.
The gamble pays off, both in its terrible resonance in our violent world and in her formidable creative accomplishment.
What the ever-impressive Frecknall shows is Kane’s empathy, her absolute command of atmosphere and tension on stage and her refusal to glamorise or soften the effect of cruelty.
Still, maybe Kane suits a more pared-back approach, one that lets her message cut like a knife.

Frecknall can’t seem to decide whether to show us the extremes, or to abstract them, and the result is only sometimes extraordinary, never quite living up to the version of the play that runs through your perplexed head when reading it.
Yet in the end, the piece is so extreme that it doesn’t land with the same force as, say, the blinding of Lear.

The play’s stage directions say that it’s set in a university, but that feels grimly ironic, as set designer Madeleine Girling’s grubbily nondescript slice of hallway and strip of a windowed room quickly break the boundaries of literalism to become a torture chamber of difference.
I would vehemently argue that this is not sufficient reason to subject yourself to this gruelling deluge.
Scratch away the veneer, and what’s left is a series of intense rehearsal room exercises, delivered with true professionalism, but in the end signifying nothing.
It is unarguably powerful, an embittered, howling manifesto of a world unsalvageable.
Nevertheless, it’s not an easy watch, and the violence often seems gratuitous.
Frecknall’s Almeida swansong lacks some of the coherence of her earlier work for the venue.
But the play's ambiguity blocks it from developing.
Toward the final elements of last evening’s press night performance, I determined never to put myself through the wretched torture of a Sarah Kane play, ever again.
Sadly, Cleansed was not a pleasant experience for me, though I am sure others will have wildly different takes on it and, after all, that is the beauty of theatre.

cn.t: Frecknall's revival of Kane's notoriously violent play divides critics, with some praising its expressionistic approach to extreme content while others find it relentlessly one-dimensional and meaningless despite strong performances.

vr.q: Sadly, I think Rebecca Frecknall didn't get the best out of it. So, I give this production of Sarah Kane's Cleansed three stars.
